overview: Avar rulers and their followers established a powerful, diverse realm in the Carpathian Basin after arriving in 567-568. Its history includes settled villages, skilled metalworkers and extensive family networks as well as mounted armies. The map continues the label later than the independent khaganate.

periods.title: Arrival and expansion
periods.summary: Steppe migrants settled among existing populations; Avar campaigns against Byzantium culminated in the unsuccessful siege of Constantinople in 626.

periods.title: Settlements and communities
periods.summary: Stable settlements and large cemeteries provide evidence for Avar-period households across the Carpathian Basin.

periods.title: Political breakup
periods.summary: Frankish campaigns broke the khaganate around 800; its former inhabitants continued living under new political arrangements.

items.text: A study of four fully excavated Hungarian cemeteries reconstructed family trees extending as far as nine generations. Some 300 of the 424 sampled people had identifiable close relatives in the same cemetery: a family album assembled from ancient DNA.

In those communities, male family lines tended to remain locally rooted while women arrived from other communities. Marriage helped connect settlements. This describes the studied cemeteries, not an inflexible rule for every Avar household.

Researchers found little evidence of unions between close biological relatives. They suggest that remembering ancestry mattered across generations. DNA can reveal biological connections; adoption, affection and other social bonds require different evidence.

Leobersdorf and Modling, two seventh- and eighth-century communities near Vienna, used similar material culture but had different ancestry and marriage networks. Matching clothes or ornaments do not automatically mean that two families shared the same origins.

Environmental and archaeological research indicates expanding settlement and farming into the mid-700s. The familiar image of an entire population permanently on horseback misses the people growing food and maintaining villages.

sections.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work

items.text: The Vrap treasure was discovered in Albania in 1901 inside a copper cauldron. Its vessels, gold belt fittings and pieces of precious metal were gathered together, but that does not tell us who buried them or why.

Some Vrap belt fittings show griffins and curling vines. Casting such small, elaborate objects required careful metalworking. The museum interprets decorated belts as statements of rank, rather like formal clothing with an exceptionally expensive buckle.

The treasure includes drinking vessels, a pouring ewer and a bucket. They reveal an elite world of serving and displaying precious metal; they are not a picture of the tableware in every village home.

The Met now labels the ensemble Avar or Byzantine. Proposed explanations include a leader's wealth or a craftworker's materials, and scholars disagree over where some pieces were made. Those uncertainties are part of the discovery.

The eighth-century Ewer of Zenobius has five marks imitating Byzantine official stamps. Examination shows they were engraved, not struck. A convincing-looking quality mark is a clue to investigate, not automatic proof of origin.

The Zenobius ewer carries a Greek inscription, possibly copied from a Byzantine model by an Avar craftworker. Greek letters on a valued object do not establish the language spoken in the owner's household.

Other Avar-period objects have short runiform inscriptions. Their readings remain disputed, including the Szarvas example. A confidently translated sentence in an imagined Avar language would conceal how much is still unresolved.

ending.text: Charlemagne's campaigns in the 790s and early 800s dismantled Avar political power. People and local traditions continued within neighbouring societies. The map's later Avar label is not evidence that an independent khaganate survived to 1000.

sources.note: Abstract and Main: Leobersdorf and Modling, seventh- to eighth-century cemeteries, 722 individuals; shared culture did not imply identical ancestry or marriage networks.

sources.note: Pages 2-3, discussion of Szarvas-Nagyszentmiklos and other Avar-period inscriptions; sound values and language remain undeciphered. A scholarly objection, not a Unicode endorsement of any decipherment.

sources.title: Johannes Preiser-Kapeller: The Climate of the Khagan (2018)
sources.note: Research abstract: environmental, written and archaeological evidence indicates growth in settlement and agricultural activity up to the middle eighth century; climate causation remains interpretive.
